query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment.
papers.approach: CALPHAD analyses, non‐equilibrium solidification simulations, and diffusion‐driven precipitation modeling combined with casting and heat-treatment experiments
papers.findings: For the Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, a soft FCC phase forms first during solidification while, in the Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8 system, intermetallic compounds (e.g., Mg2Si, Al9Mn2Si) appear early. Post‐solidification diffusion simulations indicated that the evolution of intermetallic precipitates occurs at higher concentrations of reactive elements.
papers.mechanism: Diffusion‐driven precipitation from a non-equilibrium, predominantly solid-solution state leads to the formation and growth of intermetallic phases that ultimately impact mechanical and, by implication, corrosion/oxidation behavior.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg⁴TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.system: Mg–Ti–Zn alloys processed by high-energy ball milling (HEBM) and spark plasma sintering (SPS)
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering; characterization by XRD, SEM, STEM, potentiodynamic polarization, immersion tests, and XPS
papers.findings: Both equal-molar MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ) alloys exhibited high hardness and stiffness as well as enhanced corrosion resistance. The improved corrosion response was correlated with the formation of a Ti-rich passive surface layer (e.g., TiO2 film).
papers.mechanism: Controlled non-equilibrium processing leads to a multiphase structure where reactive elements like Ti segregate to the surface and form passivating oxide films, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.

papers.title: Microstructure, Phase Formation and Heat-Treating of Novel Cast Al-Mg-Zn-Cu-Si Lightweight Complex Concentrated Aluminum Based Alloy.
papers.system: An Al–Mg–Zn–Cu–Si alloy with a density near 2.63 g/cm³
papers.approach: Design using CALPHAD and thermo-physical evaluation; cast production via induction furnace and pour mold casting; heat treatment studies with microstructural and mechanical characterization
papers.findings: The alloy develops a multiphase microstructure with a dominant α-Al matrix and various intermetallic phases (e.g., Mg₂Si, Al₂Cu). Heat treatment leads to modifications in hardness, compressive strength, and electrical conductivity; the presence and distribution of intermetallics appears key to its performance.
papers.mechanism: Non-equilibrium solidification in a multicomponent system leads to a metastable state that subsequently evolves via controlled precipitation of intermetallic phases, affecting both corrosion (through passivation behavior) and high-temperature oxidation response.

papers.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Lightweight quinary HEAs (e.g., AlBeMgTiLi, AlBeMgTiSi, AlBeMgTiCu) with target densities below 5 g/cm³
papers.approach: High-throughput first-principles calculations (PSSOS), exploring formation energy vs. density and elastic properties across a four-dimensional compositional grid
papers.findings: Identified topmost compositions that balance low density, high elastic modulus, and energetic stability; demonstrated that metastable solid-solution states can be realized, though they might be sensitive to elemental substitutions (e.g., substitution of reactive elements may promote intermetallic formation).
papers.mechanism: A trade-off exists between stability (as determined by formation energy) and the tendency to form intermetallic compounds upon relaxation from a non-equilibrium state, which in turn can modify surface oxide formation and corrosion resistance.

papers.title: Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlxCoCrFeNi and related HEAs containing Al in a predominantly BCC (or mixed FCC/BCC) matrix
papers.approach: Combined Monte Carlo simulations informed by first-principles parameters; CALPHAD predictions, and comparison with in situ and ex situ experimental observations (e.g., neutron scattering, microscopy)
papers.findings: Non-equilibrium solidification leads to a state that is disordered at high temperatures and then orders on cooling – with Al segregating to one sublattice. The onset of ordering and subsequent phase evolution depend on the Al content and thermal history, which implies that metastable states may evolve over time.
papers.mechanism: Temperature-dependent ordering within initially non-equilibrium solid solution leads to phase separation, where elemental segregation (including that of light elements such as Mg in related systems) directs the formation of ordered intermetallic phases, potentially altering corrosion and oxidation behavior.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy as a model system for complex alloys
papers.approach: Controlled oxidation experiments at 400 °C under defined oxygen pressures; in situ atom probe tomography (APT), TEM, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) measurements
papers.findings: Revealed layered oxide film formation with a Ni-enriched base, followed by Cr-rich and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers. The study highlights how redox potentials and atomic diffusion during solid-state oxidation lead to the development and evolution of passivating oxide layers.
papers.mechanism: Initial oxidation stages follow both atomic size and redox potential arguments – with the initial formation of a pre-oxide layer that segues into distinct compositional layers. Although studied in a different system, similar mechanisms of atomic diffusion and selective oxidation in a non-equilibrium state could dictate oxidation evolution in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.

papers.title: Characterisation of a Novel Complex Concentrated Alloy for Marine Applications.
papers.system: Al–Cu–Si–Zn–Mg based complex concentrated alloy aimed at marine applications
papers.approach: Casting combined with heat treatment; CALPHAD simulations; comprehensive structural, mechanical, and corrosion testing
papers.findings: The developed alloy exhibits a dendritic structure with a predominant Al-rich phase and significant formation of intermetallic compounds (e.g., Al₂Cu) that contribute to high yield strength and corrosion resistance in chloride-rich environments.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between primary solid solution formation and subsequent precipitation of intermetallic phases under non-equilibrium conditions leads to a microstructure that enhances mechanical resistance and corrosion performance due to a controlled distribution of phases.

established: Lightweight HEAs and complex concentrated alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ can be designed from common, low-density elements (e.g., Mg, Al, Zn).
Non-equilibrium processing (casting, ball milling + SPS) often leads to metastable solid-solution states that evolve via precipitation of intermetallic phases.
Intermetallic compounds, even if thermodynamically stable at higher concentrations, can be beneficial for mechanical properties if they are uniformly distributed at a nanoscale.
Corrosion and oxidation behaviors are strongly influenced by the formation of passivating oxide films, often promoted by alloying additions (e.g., Ti forming TiO₂).

approaches_tried.approach: Induction melting and casting with post-heat treatments
approaches_tried.outcome: Generated multiphase microstructures; heat treatment altered the balance between solid solution and intermetallic phases, affecting mechanical and corrosion properties.

approaches_tried.approach: High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS)
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced refined, non-equilibrium structures with enhanced hardness and corrosion resistance via formation of protective, passive surface films.

Mapped the compositional space of lightweight HEAs, predicting metastable regions and optimal compositions balancing low density and high stiffness, though discrepancies with experimental phase distributions exist.

mechanisms: Diffusion-driven precipitation from a non-equilibrium solid solution leading to intermetallic phase formation.
Elemental segregation during rapid solidification which later promotes the formation of passivating oxide layers (e.g., Ti-rich oxides).
Temperature-induced ordering transitions in initially supersaturated phases that alter the microstructure and surface chemistry, thereby influencing oxidation and corrosion responses.
disagreements: Some simulations (e.g., CALPHAD, Monte Carlo) predict a higher number of phases or differing phase distributions than those observed experimentally, indicating uncertainty in diffusion kinetics and elemental partitioning in multicomponent systems.
The role of specific alloying elements (e.g., Mg versus Ti) in the formation of protective films during high-temperature oxidation remains debated between studies focusing on different systems.
open_questions: How exactly does the evolution from a metastable solid-solution state to a precipitated intermetallic structure alter the kinetics and nature of passive film formation under corrosive and high-temperature conditions?
What is the effect of varying Mg content on the balance between desirable mechanical properties and the tendency to form stable, but potentially detrimental, intermetallic compounds?
Which microstructural length scales (e.g., precipitate size and distribution) are most critical for modulating both corrosion behavior and high-temperature oxidation resistance?
opportunities: Design experiments that directly compare the corrosion and oxidation behavior of as-cast (metastable state) vs. heat-treated (transformed intermetallic structure) Mg-containing lightweight HEAs under identical environmental exposures.
Utilize rapid cooling and controlled annealing treatments to finely tune the onset and extent of intermetallic precipitation, thereby correlating structural evolution with surface film formation.

Integrate in situ characterization techniques (such as APT, in situ TEM/oxidation studies) to track real-time phase evolution and the development of passivating layers in non-equilibrium processed alloys.

Leverage combined computational and experimental approaches to optimize the concentration window of Mg and other reactive elements to achieve both high specific strength and improved resistance to corrosion/oxidation.

directions.direction: Tailor composition by varying Mg and supplementary reactive elements to directly suppress or encourage the formation of specific intermetallic compounds that may affect oxide scale formation.
directions.assessment: This approach would test how different elemental ratios change phase stability but may not isolate the non-equilibrium evolution pathway. It is supported by computational design studies (see PMC10728166::web::052::energetical_stability) yet the complexity of multicomponent interactions makes it challenging to directly connect composition with specific corrosion/oxidation changes.

directions.direction: Utilize rapid solidification (casting) followed by controlled post‐annealing to trigger a diffusion‐driven precipitation of intermetallic phases that alter local chemistry and the nature of oxide film formation.
directions.assessment: This approach directly addresses the evolution from a metastable state. Evidence (PMC7579168::web::035::5_conclusions, PMC9100001::web::004::1_introduction) supports that diffusion‐driven precipitation occurs in these systems and affects both mechanical and surface oxidation properties. The intervention is highly feasible and allows a controlled comparison between as-cast and annealed states.

directions.direction: Apply surface treatments that promote selective elemental segregation (e.g., via ion implantation or laser surface melting) to enhance formation of protective oxide layers.
directions.assessment: While surface modification can improve corrosion and oxidation resistance, it does not directly probe the intrinsic evolution of the non-equilibrium alloy’s bulk microstructure, and may introduce additional variables that obscure the mechanistic pathway.

directions.direction: Perform in situ real-time characterization (e.g., using APT, in situ TEM) during oxidation and corrosion tests to capture the phase evolution and oxide scale formation directly.
directions.assessment: This would provide excellent insight into the kinetics and mechanisms. However, despite its high informativity, the in situ approach is technically challenging and may not readily allow a controlled comparison with a well-defined starting state.

directions.direction: Employ computational modelling (CALPHAD combined with diffusion kinetics simulations) to predict the evolution of metastable phases and correlate those changes with changes in predicted corrosion/oxidation behavior.
directions.assessment: Modelling can guide understanding of phase evolution and predict the effect on oxide formation. Still, such predictions need experimental validation and may not capture kinetic barriers in real systems where rapid processing is used.

choice.direction: Utilize rapid solidification followed by controlled post‐annealing to trigger diffusion‐driven precipitation
choice.why: This direction most directly isolates the evolution from a non-equilibrium metastable state to a precipitated microstructure, thereby linking the diffusion‐driven formation of intermetallic particles with modifications in local chemistry. Such microstructural changes are expected to modify the nucleation and growth of protective oxides, affecting both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior. The approach is supported by multiple studies (e.g., PMC7579168::web::035::5_conclusions, PMC9100001::web::004::1_introduction, PMC12299034::web::035::4_conclusions) and is feasible as a controlled comparison between as-cast and annealed conditions.
